argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0101d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0101.

PROJECT
The team is designing a voice-controlled kitchen timer.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomas  present
B  Marketing Expert (ME)  Grace  present
C  User Interface designer (UI)  Ravi  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Helen  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0101a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, introduced the team and presented the project: a voice-controlled kitchen timer that sits on the counter and can be operated hands-free. She presented the budget: a selling price of 25 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit, and a profit target of 50 million euros. The team discussed the target group and first features. The final target group is home cooks. This replaced an earlier choice of professional kitchens, which the team revised because of the price point and the kitchen noise. The user interface designer raised the wake word problem, the alarm, and a simple display. The industrial designer pointed out that a custom wake word and a spoken alarm would increase the hardware cost. The project manager assigned research tasks to each team member. The next meeting, the functional design meeting, is in thirty minutes.
  decisions: The target group is home cooks in ordinary households. This was revised during the meeting from an earlier choice of professional kitchens. The timer will support multiple named timers. The display will use large, readable digits rather than a colour screen. The timer will have a physical button fallback in case voice commands are not recognised. The team will meet again in thirty minutes for the functional design meeting.
  actions: The marketing expert will research what home cooks need from a kitchen timer, possibly with a quick survey. The industrial designer will investigate voice recognition chips and whether they fit within the 12.50 euro production cost. He will also look at battery versus mains power. The user interface designer will work out the wake word, the voice commands (set, cancel, time remaining), the display and a button fallback. The project manager will send round the minutes.
  problems: It is unknown whether a voice recognition chip fits within the 12.50 euro production cost. The power source (battery or mains) is undecided, because always-on listening consumes power. It is undecided whether the wake word will be fixed or user-selectable. A user-selectable wake word needs a more expensive chip. It is undecided whether the alarm will announce which timer finished or only beep. A spoken alarm needs a speaker and adds cost. The device should be easy to clean and at least splash-proof, but this has not been specified further.
  action item SY0101a.ai1: Research user requirements for the kitchen timer among home cooks, possibly through a quick survey. This was originally assigned as research into chefs' needs. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0101a.ai2: Investigate available voice recognition chips and their cost relative to the 12.50 euro production budget, including battery versus mains power. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0101a.ai3: Design the wake word, the voice commands (set, cancel, time remaining), the display and a button fallback. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0101a.ai4: Send round the minutes of the kickoff meeting. (owner D, active)
  fact (plan_change): The team first agreed to target professional kitchens and restaurants. Later in the meeting they changed the target to home cooks, because of the 25 euro price point and the noise in professional kitchens.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed letting users choose their own wake word. This was not agreed because of the chip cost.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer suggested a fixed wake word to allow a cheap chip. The project manager only said to keep it in mind.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a spoken alarm that announces which timer is done. This was left open because it needs a speaker.

[SY0101b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting, noted that the user interface designer was absent because he had been called into a user testing session for another project, and confirmed that the kickoff minutes had been sent round. The marketing expert presented the results of an online survey of twenty-three home cooks: users want to avoid touching the device with dirty hands, often lose track of which of several timers is going off, need an alarm loud enough to be heard over an extractor fan, want an easy-to-clean device and do not want to change batteries often. The industrial designer compared a fixed vocabulary voice chip (about 2.80 euros) with a trainable chip that allows a user-chosen wake word (about 6.50 euros). The team chose the fixed vocabulary chip with a fixed wake word, and limited named timers to a fixed list of about ten names because the chip recognises only about forty words. The team also agreed on a spoken alarm that beeps and then says the timer's name, using a small speaker of about 1.20 euros, so that voice input and output together cost about four euros. For power, the team first leaned towards three AA batteries but switched to mains power with a USB adapter after the industrial designer calculated that always-on listening would drain the batteries in about three weeks. The project manager will inform the absent user interface designer of the decisions.
  decisions: The timer will use a fixed vocabulary voice recognition chip (about 2.80 euros) rather than a trainable chip. The wake word will be fixed and not user-selectable. Named timers will use a fixed list of up to about ten names. The alarm will beep and then speak the name of the finished timer, using a small speaker. The timer will be mains-powered with a USB adapter instead of batteries. Splash-proofing and easy cleaning will be dealt with in the conceptual design meeting together with the casing materials.
  actions: The marketing expert will choose the list of about ten timer names from the survey results. This task was first intended for the user interface designer. The industrial designer will get proper price quotes for the speaker and for a small backup battery. The project manager will email the absent user interface designer the decisions on the fixed wake word, the timer name list and the alarm, including the chip prices behind the wake word decision. The user interface designer will continue working on the voice commands, the display and the button fallback for the conceptual design meeting.
  problems: The cost of a small backup battery is unknown, and it is not decided whether one will be included. The speaker price of about 1.20 euros has not been confirmed with a proper quote. The splash-proof and easy-to-clean casing has not yet been specified. The user interface designer has not yet been told about the decisions, and the effect of the fixed vocabulary on the button fallback is still open.
  action item SY0101b.ai1: Choose the list of about ten timer names from the survey answers on what home cooks time most. (owner B, reassigned)
  action item SY0101b.ai2: Get proper price quotes for the speaker and for a small backup battery. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0101b.ai3: Email the absent user interface designer the decisions (fixed wake word, timer names coming from the marketing expert, spoken alarm), including the chip prices explaining the wake word decision. (owner D, active)
  action item SY0101b.ai4: Continue working on the voice commands, the display and the button fallback for the conceptual design meeting. (owner C, active)
  fact (absence): The user interface designer (Ravi) was absent because he had been pulled into a user testing session for another project.
  fact (plan_change): The team first agreed on battery power with three AA batteries, then switched to mains power with a USB adapter because always-on listening would drain the batteries in about three weeks.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer suggested adding a small backup battery so that timers are kept if the device is unplugged. This was not decided and will be costed first.

[SY0101c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting and welcomed back the user interface designer, who confirmed that he had received her email with the decisions and chip prices from the functional design meeting. The marketing expert presented the list of ten timer names taken from the survey: pasta, rice, eggs, potatoes, vegetables, roast, oven, bread, cake and tea. The user interface designer showed that the names, the wake word, four commands and the number words use exactly the forty words the chip can recognise, and the team kept all ten names. The industrial designer reported a speaker quote of 1.40 euros, which brings voice input and output to 4.20 euros, and a backup battery quote of about 0.90 euros against an estimated unit cost of about 11.10 euros. The team left the backup battery out for now. The user interface designer presented a backlit segment LCD with large digits and printed icons for the timer names. The team rejected his touch strip in favour of a rotary dial with a separate cancel button. For the casing, the team chose a splash-proof, wipe-clean ABS body with rubber seals and a flat display window, available in white and black.
  decisions: All ten timer names from the marketing expert's list are kept, which uses the chip's full forty-word vocabulary, so no words can be added later. The speaker costs 1.40 euros, so voice input and output together cost 4.20 euros. The backup battery is left out for now and may be added back if the final costing leaves room. The display will be a backlit segment LCD that shows one timer in large digits, with printed icons for the timer names and for other running timers. The button fallback will be a rotary dial (turn to set, push to start, push and hold to choose a timer) plus a separate cancel button. The touch strip was rejected. The casing will be an ABS plastic body with rubber seals around the dial and button and a flat display window. It will be splash-proof and wipe-clean, but not dishwasher safe. The timer will come in white and black.
  actions: The industrial designer and the user interface designer will build a mock-up model of the casing with the dial and the display for the detailed design meeting. The industrial designer will prepare a full cost breakdown, including whether the backup battery fits the budget. The user interface designer will write up the final forty-word vocabulary list with example phrases and decide the alarm wording. The marketing expert will put together evaluation criteria from the survey to check the design against. The project manager will send round the minutes.
  problems: The vocabulary is at the chip's limit of forty words, so there is no room to add any commands or names later. The estimated unit cost of about 11.10 euros leaves little margin, and whether the 0.90 euro backup battery can be included depends on the full cost breakdown. A third colour, such as sage green, is still open. The marketing expert's idea of a fridge magnet was not adopted because of the mains cable, and is only being kept in mind. The exact alarm wording (for example 'pasta is done') is not yet decided.
  action item SY0101c.ai1: Build a mock-up model of the casing with the dial and the display for the detailed design meeting, together with the user interface designer. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0101c.ai2: Prepare a full cost breakdown of the timer, including whether the backup battery fits the budget. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0101c.ai3: Write up the final forty-word vocabulary list with example phrases and decide the alarm wording. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0101c.ai4: Put together evaluation criteria from the survey to check the design against. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0101c.ai5: Send round the minutes of the conceptual design meeting. (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested dropping one or two timer names to leave spare vocabulary. The marketing expert objected and it was not adopted.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer argued for including the backup battery so timers survive unplugging. The team did not adopt it for now.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed a touch strip for setting minutes. It was rejected because of wet and dirty hands.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert asked whether the timer could be dishwasher safe. The industrial designer said this is not possible with electronics inside.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested a third colour such as sage green. This was left open.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a magnet on the back for fridge mounting. It was not adopted because of the mains cable and is only kept in mind.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested the alarm say 'pasta is done'. The wording was left to the user interface designer.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_OFF_TOPIC_TANGENT [F1]: A long off-topic tangent (at least 8 consecutive segments, e.g. weekend plans, a film, the coffee machine) unrelated to the project. The gold summary must NOT include the tangent's content.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_PLAN_CHANGE [F1]: The team agrees on a plan early in the meeting, then later in the same meeting changes it (different choice, date, or approach). The gold summary must state only the FINAL plan, and may mention that it was revised.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
